newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Danger for Australian wool seen in price surge.
newsitem.headline: Danger for Australian wool seen in price surge.

text.p: Australia's embattled wool industry was presented on Thursday with the prospect of a major market turnaround sufficient to confront wool with the new threat of being priced out of world markets.

The warnings, presented at opening sessions of the annual conference of the Wool Council of Australia (WCA), coincide with a three percent market surge in recent days which has pushed auction prices to the point of breaking through the 700 Australian cents/kg mark for the first time in almost two years.

The dangers of higher-priced wool, a major turnaround in perspective in an industry which has wallowed in gloomy market sentiment for years, were raised by both WCA president Rod Thirkell-Johnston and International Wool Textile Organisation (IWTO) president Henry Gnonzke.

"Unacceptable price levels could turn customers away from wool, (a matter of) increasing concern," Thirkell-Johnston said. He said this was especially so as Australia's 1.8 million bale wool stockpile was sold down toward the zero target by 2000.
The WCA president went on to say, however, that for the first time this decade the future was brighter for wool.
IWTO president Gnonzke went further to state that world consumption of merino wol in the current year would exceed production by 10 to 20 percent.
This indicated real scope for a double digit increase in Australian merino wool production, he said.

Gnonzke, who also called for a new flat-rate levy of two percent a kg at point of export on wool sales to fund a major international new promotion drive, said wool's price was presently at a ratio of 3.4 to synthetics.
"This is already on the high side and pressure on costs will remain ... into the forseeable future," he said.

Gnonzke said over-use of pesticides or abuse of unregistered pesticides was also already a further disencentive to use of wool in the developed woprld. This would undoubtedly spread to many parts of the less developed world, he said.
He called for the bulk of the world merino clip to be shipped in non-contaminant re-cyclable packs by year 2000.

A new drive for research and development, product innovation and advertising would require additional annual funding of A$80 million, to be financed by the proposed two percent levy at export, he said.

Efforts by IWTO to raise this through voluntary schemes had been in vain because of refusal by producing countries, he said. "The structure of our industry requires that we discuss our promotion levy in ... public ... whereas our competitors, the chemical giants, have huge amounts included in their budgets for promotion and yet can keep details confidential," he said.
Additional funds would be used predominantly for joint-ventures with industry, which would supply additional funding in a ratio of 2.5 in China to up to 5.0 in Europe.
Through this, the A$80 million would become A$200 million or more, he said. Floor questions from Australian growers at the conference indicated reluctance to pay a new levy.
In his address, Gnonzke described the Scottish cloned sheep Dolly as the "souffle" of the meal he was presenting to the WCA conference.

"The cloning of sheep for agricultural purposes is clearly some way off, and many questions remain to be answered, not least of which is whether flocks of identical sheep would not replicate genetic weaknesses and be much more prone to disease," he said.

"Nevertheless, one message is clear - the door has now been opened for the sheep industry to develop elite flocks, with the potential to produce wool types required by consumer-driven demand," Gnonzke said.
